paragraphs:
Natan deTzutzita. Shabbat 56b: Rav says none among penitents was greater than Yoshiyah in his generation; in ours, Abba, R. Yirmeyah bar Abba's father; some say Aḥa, father of Abba, R. Yirmeyah's father. R. Yosef adds another in our generation, Ukva bar Neḥemyah the exilarch, namely Natan deTzutzita. R. Yosef sat dozing at the lecture and dreamed that [the angel] reached out and accepted him. Rashi explains Tzutzita from the angel's grasping his hair. Tosafot says Rabbenu Tam found a midrash about a lamp burning on his head; Rashi likewise in Dinei Mamonot. It is not there but at the end of Zeh Borer 31b: they sent Mar Ukva, 'To him whose radiance resembles Batyah's son'—Moshe—'peace; Ukvan the Babylonian complained before us,' etc. Rashi: his face radiated like Moshe, raised by Pharaoh's daughter Batyah; alternatively, his wisdom illuminated his face. He found an aggadic book: Mar Ukva desired a married woman and fell ill; later she needed a loan and in distress consented. He mastered his impulse, sent her away peacefully and recovered. When he went out, a heavenly lamp shone on his head, hence Natan deTzutzita in Shabbat 56. The letter likewise alluded to that light. End of quotation. Rashi says Mar Ukva was court head, BaMeh Vehemah.

The geonim say he curled his hair in youth. They also say a tongue of fire issued from his locks, driving those sitting before him away; see She'iltot, VaEra and Ki Tissa. Arukh, Natan: the name refers to the fiery-spark angel who extended a hand and accepted his repentance. Alternatively he wore a goat-hair shirt scratching his flesh as penitential atonement. End of quotation. Yuḥasin, under ayin, calls Mar Ukva court head in Shemuel's days, a penitent with light upon his head, Natan deTzutzita. This is impossible: Natan was before Rav Yosef, Mar Ukva before Shemuel. Perhaps there were two; the truth is that Natan was (Abba), R. Yirmeyah's father. End of quotation. That 'truth' is false: Rav Yosef explicitly adds Ukvan bar Neḥemyah the exilarch, namely Natan, whose hair the angel grasped. Rashi's claim that court head Mar Ukva was this penitent requires examination: Shabbat specifies Ukvan bar Neḥemyah, exilarch in Rav Yosef's time, not Mar Ukva. Bava Batra 55a: Rabbah received three statements from Ukvan bar Neḥemyah in Shemuel's name. Rabbah and his colleague Rav Yosef were Rav Yehudah's students, and Rav Yehudah was Shemuel's student; thus Ukvan was exilarch in Rav and Rav Yosef's days [source wording retained], while Mar Ukva headed court in Shemuel's days. They certainly differ. Perhaps Rashi's aggadic book mistakenly read Mar Ukva for Ukvan bar Neḥemyah. I found Natan in R. Akiva's time, in R. Nissim son of R. Yaakov's storybook for his son-in-law Dunash 37a, as follows:

A wealthy man named Natan deTzutzita loved a married woman, Ḥannah. Her husband was very poor; she was exceedingly beautiful. Natan became ill from his desire. Physicians said only lying with him would cure him; Israel's sages said he must die rather than transgress. They proposed that she come speak with him; the sages refused. His illness grew long. Her husband had many debts and was imprisoned. She spun day and night to buy him bread. After long imprisonment he despaired of life. He told her that saving one life was like sustaining many; she should pity him, ask Natan for a loan and redeem him. She answered that Natan lay dying because of her; every day his messengers offered much money, which she refused, forbidding their return. How could she now seek a loan? Had imprisonment driven him mad? She left angrily and did not visit.

On the fourth day she pitied him and went to see him before he died. Finding him near death, she heard him accuse her: God would demand redress and hold her guilty; she wished him dead so she could marry Natan. She told him to divorce and release her, and she would go to Natan. He said this proved her desire. She cried aloud and fell on her face: who had heard of telling a woman to commit adultery and become impure to free her husband? He told her to leave him until God pitied him. At home she considered both their distress, pitied him and prayed for rescue from transgression. She went to Natan. His eunuchs hurried to announce her at the gate; he promised them freedom if true. In the courtyard his maid announced her; he promised her freedom too. He asked Ḥannah what she wanted and promised to grant it. She asked a specified loan for her imprisoned husband, a righteous deed before God. His servants rushed to give it.

Natan said he had fulfilled her wish; knowing his illness from love, she should now fulfill his and revive him. She answered: she was in his hands, beneath his wings, unable to oppose him, but he now had an opportunity to acquire the world to come. He must not lose its reward and goodness for a small thing, nor make her forbidden to her husband. He should imagine his desire satisfied rather than lose great good and remain regretful when it ended; remember the punishments God inflicts and avoid later remorse. By brief restraint he could gain long life and reward in this world and the next, ordinarily won with great labor. Listening to reason and rebuking his impulse could win his Creator's favor in an instant. Hearing her, he rebuked his evil impulse, rose from bed, fell on his face and prayed to subdue desire, walk rightly, receive forgiveness and repent completely. God answered. He blessed Ḥannah and her judgment for preventing bloodshed and sin; her hands had saved him. He sent her home in peace. She redeemed her husband and told him, but he suspected she concealed intercourse with Natan.

Later R. Akiva looked from a window and saw a horseman with brilliant sunlight upon his head. Asked his identity, a student answered, 'Natan, the herder of prostitutes.' Akiva asked whether they saw anything upon his head; they did not. He summoned Natan and told him he saw great light and knew him an heir to the world to come: what had he done? Natan told Ḥannah's words. R. Akiva marveled at his restraint, submission and full repentance. He said his great deed had brought this radiance in this world, all the more in the next; he should sit before him to learn Torah. He did so; the One who opens and none shuts opened his heart's doors to Torah. Soon he reached great wisdom and sat beside R. Akiva at one rank. Ḥannah's husband passed R. Akiva's academy, saw Natan at his side, asked a student how he had risen so high, and heard the whole story. He now believed Ḥannah; his jealous suspicion ceased. At home he kissed her head and asked forgiveness for suspecting her until seeing Natan beside R. Akiva and hearing his deeds. May God multiply her reward doubly: he had been deeply troubled until God's mercy revealed this today. End of quotation.

On this basis one may answer why Ukvan bar Neḥemyah was called Natan deTzutzita, rather than Ukvan bar Neḥemyah Tzutzita, from the fiery sparks. Natan in R. Akiva's time was called Tzutzita for the light; Ukvan too, having light, was named after Natan. The God of truth knows the truth. A parallel is Yesh Noḥalin: Yonatan ben Gershom ben Menashe was actually Moshe's grandson; having acted like Menashe, wrongdoing was attached to the wrongdoer. Maharsha’s Ḥiddushei Aggadot adds: as Menashe wholeheartedly repented, so Yonatan repented; see there. End of BaMeh Vehemah compares earlier and later figures, praising them for deeds the later ones did not do, etc. Another explanation: Rav Yosef says another penitent in our generation was Ukvan bar Neḥemyah, 've-hainu Natan deTzutzita,' rather than 'hu Natan.' Elsewhere: Abba bar Marta 'is' Abba bar Minyomi; Yosef of Hutzal 'is' Yosef the Babylonian, Issi ben Gur Aryeh, Issi ben Gamliel and Issi ben Mahalalel (see his entry); R. Yitzḥak ben Tavla 'is' R. Yitzḥak ben Ḥakla and R. Yitzḥak son of R. Ilai (see his entry). Here ve-hainu means Ukvan's light resembled Natan's, etc.

See Yuḥasin, after the epistle of R.Sh.G. [רש״ג; provisionally Rav Sherira Gaon], the brief generations from Yehudah, etc., to Yehoyakhin: Neḥemyah, Meshullam, Ḥananyah, Berekhya, Ḥasadya, Yeshayah, Ovadyah, Shekhanyah, Shemayah, Ḥizkiyah, Yoḥanan, Shafat, Akhan, Natan deTzutzita, Huna, Natan, Neḥemyah, Ukva, Abba bar Huna, Natan, Mar Zutra, Meremar, Kahana, Huna, Mar Zutra, Huna, Mar Kafnai, Bustanai, Ḥasdai, Shelomoh the exilarch, David ben Zakkai, who disputed with our teacher Saadyah of Fayyum. End of quotation. See Yuḥasin, from Yesod Olam with Rema's glosses, and part 1, year 4757, and what I wrote there.
